title: AI Security Engineer Foundations + Certificate — Micah Silverman, Snyk
talk_summary: A two-hour Snyk security curriculum covering OWASP LLM Top 10, shadow AI, AI-BOM, threat modeling, MCP risks, and red teaming, with a live chatbot CTF demo. Most content is security education, but a few mechanisms (AI-BOM baseline diffing in CI, adversarial cross-model review, least-privilege data views, output-as-input sanitization) are directly copyable.

takeaways.technique: AI-BOM baseline diff as a CI gate
takeaways.what_they_do: Snapshot the inventory of models/datasets/MCP servers/skills in a project as a baseline; on every commit regenerate the inventory and fail the build if it differs from the baseline, so any new AI component requires an approved baseline update.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we're going to run the AI bomb and if what it produces differs from the baseline, we're going to fail the build

takeaways.what_they_do: Generate an architecture/plan with one model, then feed those assumptions to a different vendor's model as an adversarial reviewer; the second model reliably finds weaknesses the first missed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it feeds it into uh co uh codeex or chat GBT and that becomes an adversarial review and every single time it's come up with a weakness

takeaways.technique: Least-privilege data view instead of prompt-based access control
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than telling the model in the system prompt not to reveal sensitive fields, give it a database view or synced copy that physically lacks those fields, so it cannot leak what it never had.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we're going to create a database view or we're going to have an alternate database that's kept in sync that doesn't have any of that identifying information

takeaways.technique: Treat model output as untrusted input; sanitize before downstream use
takeaways.what_they_do: Any LLM output that feeds another tool, agent, or shell must be sanitized like user input; they show a real MCP server where an unsanitized URL argument concatenated into a curl command gave shell injection.
takeaways.evidence_quote: outputs need to be sanitized in the same way that inputs do. If you're passing that output downstream, well, now that output has become an input

takeaways.technique: Excessive-agency guardrails: no direct production access, human approval for destructive ops
takeaways.what_they_do: Non-negotiables: agents never touch production directly (only via approved CI/CD), mandatory human approval for deploys/destructive ops/privilege changes, sandboxed execution, network segmentation. Cites an agent that deleted hundreds of emails despite a memory-file rule forbidding it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: AI agents never touch production directly, only indirectly, potentially through approved CI/CD pipelines

takeaways.technique: Scan/vet MCP servers and skills before install
takeaways.what_they_do: MCP servers and agent skills are just code with tool descriptions the model treats as authoritative; they scan MCP config files and skill definitions for hidden instructions/tool poisoning before use, and note 37% of registry skills had a security flaw.
takeaways.evidence_quote: 37% of them had at least one uh significant security flaw and about 13% of them had critical issue
takeaways.numbers: 37% of ~4,000 skills had a security flaw; 13% critical
